title: Normative human walking reference for the procedural gait layer
cycle_convention: Percent of gait cycle, 0 = heel strike (initial contact) of the reference foot, 100 = its next heel strike; 21 samples at 0,5,...,100. Same-side conventions: every table is for the reference side (left and right averaged after each was normalised to its own cycle).
provenance_note: Numbers marked basis "dataset mean" were computed here from the downloaded open datasets (scripts not in repo; method described per table). Numbers marked "tabulated" are copied from the cited table. Nothing here is read from a figure unless it says so. Inferences are in modifiers[*].inference and are not evidence.

sources.citation: Fukuchi CA, Fukuchi RK, Duarte M (2018). A public dataset of overground and treadmill walking kinematics and kinetics in healthy individuals. PeerJ 6:e4640. Data: figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.5722711 (version 6 files WBDSascii.zip, WBDSinfo.csv).
sources.what: USED. 42 adults with overground comfortable-speed data (24 young 21-37 y: 14 M, 10 F; 18 older 50-84 y: 10 M, 8 F). Processed *walkOCang.txt (Visual3D, per-subject ensemble mean, 101 points; Z component = sagittal) for pelvis/hip/knee/ankle/foot angles; *walkOCknt.txt vertical GRF for toe-off; raw *walkO??[SCF]mkr.txt marker trajectories (150 Hz) for spatiotemporal values, heel/MT1 heights, pelvis-centre excursions.

sources.citation: Horst F, Lapuschkin S, Samek W, Mueller K-R, Schoellhorn WI (2019). A public dataset of overground walking kinetics and full-body kinematics in healthy adult individuals. Mendeley Data v3, doi:10.17632/svx74xcrjr.3; article: Explaining the unique nature of individual gait patterns with deep learning. Scientific Reports 9:2391, doi:10.1038/s41598-019-38748-8.
sources.what: USED. 57 young adults (29 F, 28 M; mean age 23.1 y), self-selected overground walking, 54-marker full-body set at 250 Hz (Gait_rawdata_tsv.zip). Used for shoulder-line and pelvis rotation, arm (shoulder) sagittal swing, elbow flexion, trunk lean. 1123 strides.

sources.citation: Zeni JA Jr, Richards JG, Higginson JS (2008). Two simple methods for determining gait events during treadmill and overground walking using kinematic data. Gait & Posture (2008). Volume/pages not verified here (PMC page was behind a browser check); the method is as widely described.
sources.what: Method used here to detect heel strike (heel marker most anterior to pelvis centre/sacrum) and kinematic toe-off in raw marker trials.

sources.citation: Oberg T, Karsznia A, Oberg K (1993). Basic gait parameters: reference data for normal subjects, 10-79 years of age. Journal of Rehabilitation Research and Development 30(2):210-223.
sources.what: Tabulated speed, step length, step frequency at normal speed by sex and decade (15 per cell, Swedish adults). Tables 2a/b, 5a/b, 8a/b.

sources.citation: Bohannon RW, Andrews AW (2011). Normal walking speed: a descriptive meta-analysis. Physiotherapy 97(3):182-189.
sources.what: Meta-analytic normal walking speed by decade and sex. Values taken from the University of Toronto Physical Therapy handout that reproduces them: https://www.physicaltherapy.utoronto.ca/sites/default/files/assets/files/11walking-speed-age-and-sex-specific-normative-values-final.pdf

sources.citation: Perry J, Burnfield JM (2010). Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function, 2nd ed. SLACK Inc.
sources.what: Gait phase boundaries (loading response 0-12 %, midstance 12-31 %, terminal stance 31-50 % starting at heel rise, pre-swing 50-62 %, initial swing 62-75 %, mid swing 75-87 %, terminal swing 87-100 %), as reproduced by the AAPM&R PM&R KnowledgeNow page citing Perry & Burnfield. Book not consulted directly.

sources.citation: Alexander RMcN (1976). Estimation of speeds of dinosaurs. Nature (volume/pages not verified here; cited as Alexander 1976 Nature by the secondary source read).
sources.what: Dynamic-similarity stride relation lambda/h = 2.3 (v^2/(g h))^0.3, h = hip (leg) height; as quoted (eq. 1) by Ruiz & Torices 2013, which is the copy actually read.

sources.citation: Winter DA (1992). Foot trajectory in human gait: a precise and multifactorial motor control task. Physical Therapy 72:45-56 (page range as given by the citing source).
sources.what: Minimum toe clearance 1.29 cm at mid-swing, variability 0.45 cm, 11 subjects; as quoted by the citing paper (core.ac.uk PDF). Original not read.

sources.citation: Collins SH, Adamczyk PG, Kuo AD (2009). Dynamic arm swinging in human walking. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, doi:10.1098/rspb.2009.0664.
sources.what: Arms swing in opposite phase to the ipsilateral leg in normal walking (1.25 m/s); shoulder amplitudes only in a figure, not used numerically.

sources.citation: Murray MP, Sepic SB, Barnard EJ (1967). Patterns of sagittal rotation of the upper limbs in walking. Physical Therapy 47(4):272-284. doi:10.1093/ptj/47.4.272
sources.what: Classic shoulder/elbow sagittal arm-swing study. Cited for orientation only; values not retrieved.

sources.citation: Murray MP, Drought AB, Kory RC (1964). Walking patterns of normal men. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (1964); volume/pages not verified here.
sources.what: Classic reference; not read, no values used. (URL is the scilit record of the companion 1967 paper that lists it; no direct open copy found.)

sources.citation: Murray MP, Kory RC, Sepic SB (1970). Walking patterns of normal women. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation 51(11):637-650.
sources.what: Classic reference; abstract not available to us, no values used.

sources.citation: Saunders JB, Inman VT, Eberhart HD (1953). The major determinants in normal and pathological gait. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery 35-A:543-558.
sources.what: Conceptual: pelvic rotation, pelvic list, stance knee flexion, foot/ankle and knee mechanisms, lateral pelvic displacement smooth the COM path. No numbers used.

sources.citation: Kadaba MP, Ramakrishnan HK, Wootten ME (1990). Measurement of lower extremity kinematics during level walking. Journal of Orthopaedic Research, doi:10.1002/jor.1100080310 (volume/pages not verified here)
sources.what: Classic normative lower-limb kinematics; not read, no values used (cross-check target).

sources.citation: Bruijn SM et al. (2008). Coordination of leg swing, thorax rotations, and pelvis rotations during gait: the organisation of total body angular momentum. Gait & Posture (PMID 17669652).
sources.what: Pelvis-thorax coordination shifts from in-phase toward out-of-phase as speed rises (2.0-5.2 km/h, 9 men). Qualitative only. Title, journal, year and PMID from the record page; co-authors not verified here.

sources.citation: Mirelman A, Bernad-Elazari H, Nobel T, Thaler A, Peruzzi A, Plotnik M, Giladi N, Hausdorff JM (2015). Effects of aging on arm swing during gait: the role of gait speed and dual tasking. PLoS ONE 10(8):e0136043.
sources.what: Arm-swing amplitude decreases with age (groups 30-40, 41-50, 51-60, 61-77; p = 0.04), increases at fast speed. Group values are in Table 2 (image) and were NOT extracted.

sources.citation: Van Criekinge T, Truijen S, Hallemans A, Saeys W (2018). The influence of a thoracolumbosacral orthosis on gait performance in healthy adults during walking. Acta of Bioengineering and Biomechanics 20(4). doi:10.5277/ABB-01201-2018-02
sources.what: Rigid trunk orthosis (modern), 14 healthy adults: speed 1.219 -> 1.237 m/s (ns), cadence 107.9 -> 113.3 steps/min (p = 0.004), normalised stride 1.459 -> 1.432 (ns), pelvic ROM reduced in all planes (transverse about 29 %), thorax ROM changed only sagittally.

sources.citation: Nakahara K, Miyazawa Y, Yuasa M, Minamitani N, Shinmyo T, Yamamoto H (2008). Motion analysis of trunk with lumbar corset during walking in young women. ISBS 2008 conference proceedings.
sources.what: Modern lumbar corset, 6 young women, 2-D sagittal: no significant change in stride length, step frequency, speed; trunk more extended. No numbers reported.

sources.citation: Effects of experimentally increased trunk stiffness on thorax and pelvis rotations during walking. Human Movement Science, 2014 (PMID 24290610; authors not shown on the record page).
sources.what: Brace-stiffened trunk: reduced thorax-relative-to-pelvis rotation amplitude and lower thorax-pelvis relative phase. Abstract only, no numbers.

sources.citation: Chiba K, Higuchi Y (1991). The swinging properties of flared skirts in walk. Journal of Home Economics of Japan 42(7):643-653. doi:10.11428/jhej1987.42.643
sources.what: Flared skirts 42/55/68 cm long, treadmill 3.5 km/h, 3 subjects: long skirts swing periodically and largely independently of the body. Useful for the skirt agent; no gait-parameter numbers.

sources.citation: Park Y (1992). A study on the moving fitness of the tight skirt. Journal of the Ergonomics Society of Korea 11(2):57-67.
sources.what: Tight skirts in five lengths, 120 women; step and stride length measured but values not in the abstract. Long tight skirt restricts more than mini.

sources.citation: Hill TE. Hill's Manual of Social and Business Forms: a guide to correct writing. Chicago: Hill Standard Book Co., 1887 edition (section 'Etiquette in the street').
sources.what: PERIOD ADVICE, Chicago-published: "Ladies should avoid walking rapidly upon the street, as it is ungraceful and unbecoming."; "Swinging the arms when walking ... [is among the] evidences of ill-breeding in ladies."; "Allowing a dress to trail on the street is in exceedingly bad taste." (quotations from the archive.org OCR text; ellipsis and bracket ours).

sources.citation: Hall FH. The Correct Thing in Good Society. Boston: Dana Estes & Co., 1902.
sources.what: PERIOD ADVICE: "a woman who is pinched in at the waist with tight corsets, throttled around the neck with a tight collar, and cramped as to her feet with tight, high-heeled shoes, will walk about as gracefully as a swan on a turnpike-road."

sources.citation: Macfadden B. The Power and Beauty of Superb Womanhood. New York: Physical Culture Publishing Co., 1901, pp. 106-110 (quoting Anna M. Galbraith, M.D.).
sources.what: PERIOD OPINION (dress reformer): long skirts "interfere[s] with every step"; Galbraith: skirt weight and length cause an "artificial shortening of the step" plus "resisting friction of the skirts".

hip_flexion_deg.note: Hip angle of thigh relative to pelvis (Visual3D). Pelvis itself is ~10 deg anteriorly tilted, so thigh-vs-vertical is roughly hip minus tilt. Young adults; older-adult curve in alt.older.

knee_flexion_deg.note: Loading-response peak ~13.7 deg at ~13-15 %; swing peak 62.0 deg at 73 % (per-subject mean).

ankle_dorsiflexion_deg.note: Foot relative to shank, zeroed by the Visual3D model to the static standing trial. Plantarflexion peak -13.3 deg at 65 % (ensemble mean; individual peaks are larger and sharper).

foot_floor_angle_deg.note: WBDS FootAngleZ: foot segment vs laboratory, sagittal; zero ~= foot flat on the floor (it reads 0.3 to -0.7 deg over 15-30 %). +22.5 deg at heel strike, flat by ~15 %, heel rise from ~40 %, about -53 deg at toe-off (61.7 %, linearly interpolated between 60 % -46.5 and 65 % -65.2), most plantarflexed -66 deg at 66 %, back to horizontal by ~88 %.

pelvis_tilt_deg.note: Absolute pelvis vs lab (marker-defined pelvis, ~10 deg offset is the ASIS-PSIS plane, not a posture). Use only the oscillation: about 2.4 deg peak-to-peak, two cycles per stride.

pelvis_obliquity_deg.note: Sign deduced, not stated by the dataset: the positive peak (+5.5 deg at 15 %) falls in reference-side loading response, when the swing-side hip drops, so + = reference (stance) side up. Mean ROM per subject 11.3 deg.

pelvis_rotation_deg.note: Sign deduced: maximal (+6.7 deg) at 3 % when the reference limb is in front. Mean ROM per subject 13.8 deg. Horst (1.45 m/s, iliac-crest line) gives the same shape: +6.1 at 0 %, -5.8 at 53 %.

thorax_rotation_deg.unit: deg, + reference-side shoulder forward, VS LAB
thorax_rotation_deg.note: Computed from the acromion-to-acromion line (shoulder girdle, includes scapular motion; the dataset has no clean thorax markers for rotation). It is in antiphase to the pelvis: -2.0 deg at reference heel strike, +4.2 deg at 50 %. Mean ROM per subject 8.2 +/- 2.6 deg. Relative to pelvis see alt.thorax_minus_pelvis.

shoulder_flexion_deg.unit: deg, + arm forward (flexion), same side as reference foot
shoulder_flexion_deg.note: Upper arm (acromion to elbow-epicondyle midpoint) vs the trunk line (sacrum to C7) in the sagittal plane of travel. Most extended -14.9 deg at ~6 % (just after same-side heel strike), most flexed +11.0 deg at 50 %. Mean ROM per subject 26.9 +/- 10.0 deg; women 31.2, men 22.4. Arm-vs-vertical in alt.

elbow_flexion_deg.note: Angle between upper-arm (acromion-elbow) and forearm (elbow-wrist midpoint) vectors. Least flexed 20 deg at ~11 % (arm back), most flexed 51.5 deg at ~54 % (arm forward). Acromion is not the joint centre, so absolute offset is approximate; the 30 deg swing in phase with shoulder flexion is the robust part.

com_vertical_m.unit: m, relative to stride mean, + up
com_vertical_m.note: PROXY: centre of the four pelvis markers (R/L ASIS, R/L PSIS), not whole-body COM. Peak-to-peak 0.037 m; lowest at ~6 % and ~56 % (double support), highest at ~31 % and ~81 % (mid single support).

com_lateral_m.note: PROXY: pelvis-marker centre, linear drift removed per stride. Peak-to-peak 0.037 m; farthest over the reference foot at ~34 %.

heel_height_m.unit: m above the same marker in foot-flat (20-40 % median)
heel_height_m.note: Posterior calcaneus marker. Below 1 cm until ~44 %; peak 0.204 m at ~72 % (early swing, knee flexed); down again by ~95 %.

toe_height_m.unit: m above the same marker in foot-flat
toe_height_m.note: First-metatarsal-head marker (dorsum), not the toe tip. 0.077 m up at heel strike (foot toes-up), on the floor 15-60 %, swing bump 0.045 m at ~75 %, swing minimum (MTC proxy) see events.

thorax_minus_pelvis_deg.unit: deg, + reference-side shoulder forward relative to pelvis
thorax_minus_pelvis_deg.note: Shoulder line minus iliac line. ROM 19.3 deg (women 22.0, men 16.6).

arm_vs_vertical_deg.note: Upper arm vs lab vertical (no trunk correction). Hangs ~6-7 deg behind vertical on average because the trunk leans ~4.5 deg forward.

trunk_lean_deg.note: Sacrum-to-C7 line vs vertical; mean ~4.5 deg forward, ~1.5 deg oscillation twice per stride.

toe_off_pct.note: Vertical GRF below 2 % of its peak in the cycle-normalised kinetic file, young adults. Older: 62.3. Perry & Burnfield: 62 %. The marker (Zeni) method gives a later 65.6 %, a known kinematic bias.

opposite_toe_off_pct.note: Derived: own toe-off minus 50 % (symmetry; opposite heel strike measured at 50.0 %). Perry & Burnfield: 12 %.

heel_off_pct.note: First frame after 20 % where foot-floor angle falls 3 deg below its midstance value. Heel marker 10 mm above flat: 43.6 %. Perry & Burnfield put the onset of heel rise (start of terminal stance) at 31 %; visible heel rise is gradual, so pick 31-40 % for the animation and keep the heel within ~1 cm until ~44 %.

foot_flat_pct.note: Foot-floor angle reaches ~1 deg by 15 % (9.4 deg at 5 %, 1.9 at 10 %, 0.7 at 15 %). Opposite toe-off is ~12 %.

double_support_fraction.note: Two double-support periods each = toe-off minus 50 %. Perry & Burnfield ~0.20-0.24.

min_toe_clearance.note: MT1 marker swing minimum above its stance height, young. Toe-tip MTC literature value: 1.29 cm (variability 0.45 cm) at mid-swing, winter1992 (tabulated, via citing source).

arm_phase.note: Same-side arm is most extended just after same-side heel strike (~6 %) and most flexed at opposite heel strike (~50 %): arms in antiphase with the ipsilateral leg.

wbds_measured.basis: dataset mean (per-subject medians, then group mean +/- SD)
wbds_measured.method: Zeni events on raw markers; stride = heel-marker displacement HS to HS; step width = lateral heel separation at successive heel strikes; foot progression = heel to MT1/MT5 midpoint vs travel direction at 25-35 % (+ toe-out). speed_lab is the dataset's own speed column; speed_stride = stride/stride-time, ~5 % lower; use speed_stride for self-consistent animation.
wbds_measured.caveat: Older WBDS volunteers were healthy and active and walked as fast as the young; they are not a typical 1900s 60-year-old.

oberg1993_normal_speed.note: Cadence = tabulated step frequency (steps/s) x 60. SDs: speed 0.10-0.17 m/s, step 0.035-0.063 m.

horst_young_measured.note: Speed from sacrum displacement over the capture volume; German sport-science students, faster than population norms.

foot_progression_toe_out_deg.note: All 42 subjects; heel->forefoot-midpoint marker axis, so includes marker-placement offset; young women 9.0, young men 12.5.

speed_relations.basis: regression on dataset (42 subjects x slow/comfortable/fast overground, 126 points, 0.59-1.82 m/s)

froude_power_law.formula: stride_m / leg_m = C * (v / sqrt(9.81 * leg_m))^k  (leg = ASIS to medial malleolus, ~0.53 x height)

alexander1976.formula: stride / h = 2.3 * (v^2 / (9.81 * h))^0.3, h = hip height

speed_relations.use: Given speed v and figure height H: stride = H * (a + b v); cadence = 120 v / stride. Check: H = 1.70 m, v = 1.25 m/s -> stride ~1.35 m, cadence ~111 steps/min.

modifiers.legend: measured = numbers from a study or dataset; period_advice = what period books told people to do (evidence of an ideal, not of behaviour); inference = our reasoning for the animation, NOT evidence; record any use in docs/LIBERTIES.md as reconstructed.

measured.finding: Modern lumbar corset (6 young women): no significant change in stride length, step frequency or speed; trunk held more extended.

Rigid thoraco-lumbo-sacral orthosis (14 adults): speed unchanged (1.219 vs 1.237 m/s), cadence +5 % (107.9 -> 113.3 steps/min), normalised stride -2 % (ns), pelvic ROM down in all planes, transverse about -29 %; thorax ROM changed only in the sagittal plane.
Brace-stiffened trunk: smaller thorax-relative-to-pelvis rotation and more in-phase thorax-pelvis coupling (no numbers in abstract).
Long flared skirts swing periodically and largely independently of the legs (for the skirt layer, not the gait).
Long tight skirts restrict movement more than short ones; step-length values not available to us.

women_long_skirts_corsets_1890_1910.not_found: No motion-capture study of gait in a period (1890-1910) steel-boned corset with a floor-length skirt was found. All period-dress numbers below are inference.

period_advice.quote: Ladies should avoid walking rapidly upon the street, as it is ungraceful and unbecoming.
Swinging the arms when walking ... [is among the] evidences of ill-breeding in ladies.
Allowing a dress to trail on the street is in exceedingly bad taste.
... tight corsets ... tight, high-heeled shoes, will walk about as gracefully as a swan on a turnpike-road.
Galbraith: the weight and length of skirts cause an "artificial shortening of the step" plus "resisting friction of the skirts".

inference.cadence: keep the modern female cadence (do not raise it); speed falls with step length
inference.why: Step: Galbraith/Macfadden name a shorter step, Hill advises against walking fast; 0.92 is a guess within one SD of Oberg female step length. Arms: Hill calls arm-swinging ill-bred, and hands were often holding skirt, bag or parasol, so a small swing with more bent elbows. Pelvis: the -29 % transverse pelvic ROM under a rigid trunk brace (vancriekinge2018) stands in for a boned corset; thorax-pelvis counter-rotation reduced (trunkstiff2014). Trunk: upright, near 1 deg lean rather than the modern 3-4 deg (nakahara2008 found a more extended trunk). These are reconstruction choices, not measurements.

measured.finding: Healthy, active older group (50-84 y, mean 62.7) against young (21-37 y): same comfortable speed (1.27 vs 1.24 m/s), cadence +5 (113 vs 108 steps/min), knee 3 deg more flexed at heel strike (2.6 vs -0.4), plantarflexion peak at push-off 9.8 vs 13.3 deg, pelvic rotation ROM 11.6 vs 13.8 deg (-16 %), obliquity ROM 9.8 vs 11.3 deg, step width 7.4 vs 9.0 cm, lateral pelvis sway 3.2 vs 3.7 cm.
Women 60-69 against 20-29: speed 1.157 vs 1.241 m/s (-7 %), step 0.553 vs 0.591 m (-6 %). Men 60-69: speed 1.277 vs 1.227 m/s, step 0.650 vs 0.616 m (no decline in this sample).
Normal speed 60-69 against 40-49: men 1.34 vs 1.43 m/s (-6 %), women 1.24 vs 1.39 m/s (-11 %).
Arm-swing amplitude falls with age (p = 0.04); values in a table image, not extracted.

inference.why: Speed/step from Bohannon & Andrews and Oberg; ankle, knee and pelvis scales from the WBDS older-young ratios; arm swing 0.8 is a guess, because Mirelman reports a decline but we have no number. A labouring 1900s 60-year-old was probably slower than these screened volunteers; that is not sourced.

men_1900s_street_dress.not_found: No study of walking in 1900s men's dress (wool three-piece suit, leather heeled boots, hat) was found.

period_advice.quote: Upon the narrow walk, for her protection, the gentleman should generally give the lady the inside of the walk

inference.why: Shod adult men in boots walk much like today's shod men; we keep modern male norms. The 0.85 arm swing stands for coats, a cane, umbrella or parcel, or hands in pockets, and is a guess. The Chicago 1897 Edison film (README) is the way to check this.
